after.title: Preprint: Pregnancies complicated by high maternal BMI and placental inflammation have lower placental efficiency and infant Apgar scores at preterm
after.authors: Scott, H.; Bloise, E.; Connor, K. L.
after.abstract: Inflammation in pregnancy may elicit adverse pregnancy and newborn health outcomes. Obesity and chorioamnionitis are two prevalent conditions that can contribute to a pro-inflammatory environment in pregnancy. However, whether high placental inflammation identifies pregnancies complicated by maternal overweight/obesity or chorioamnionitis that are at greater risk of adverse outcomes, particularly in the absence of other major maternal comorbidities, remains unclear. Our primary objective was to examine whether high placental inflammation was associated with adverse pregnancy and neonatal outcomes in pregnancies complicated by maternal overweight/obesity or chorioamnionitis, in the absence of other major maternal comorbidities. Clinical data and placentae were obtained from 78 pregnancies across maternal prepregnancy BMI groups that delivered preterm (with and without chorioamnionitis) or term, without other major maternal comorbidities. Placental cytokine and chemokine protein expression levels were assessed by Bio-Plex immunoassay, and a pro-inflammatory summary score was derived. Placental samples with pro-inflammatory summary scores in the highest tertile were defined as having high placental inflammation, and samples with scores in the bottom two tertiles as without high inflammation. We assessed the combined effects of maternal overweight/obesity and high placental inflammation, and chorioamnionitis and high placental inflammation, on pregnancy, placental, and infant outcomes, comparing outcomes to overweight/obesity or chorioamnionitis affected pregnancies without high placental inflammation. Pregnancies complicated by maternal overweight/obesity and high placental inflammation had decreased birthweight-to-placental weight ratio (p=0.003) and lower infant Apgar scores (1-minute: p=0.03; 5-minute: p=0.01), compared to pregnancies with overweight/obesity without high placental inflammation, in preterm pregnancies only. In contrast, high placental inflammation among pregnancies with normal BMI did not associate with poorer outcomes. Chorioamnionitis cases with high placental inflammation also did not have poorer placental or infant outcomes compared to chorioamnionitis cases without high placental inflammation. Among pregnancies complicated by maternal overweight/obesity but no other major comorbidities, those with inflamed placentae may be most at risk for poor birth outcomes, particularly at preterm. Understanding placental phenotypes among sub-groups at greatest risk of adversity may allow for more targeted surveillance, early intervention, and individualised prenatal care.

after.abstract: Androgen pathway modulators (APMs) have significantly improved outcomes for men with metastatic prostate cancer, but the evolution of therapy resistance is nearly universal, and there remains a major clinical need to identify actionable vulnerabilities for therapy-resistant disease. To address this need, we employed regulatory network models that leverage multi-omic data from over 10,000 prostate cancer patients with longitudinal clinical data. Analysis of the architecture of the network models identified EP300 as the top actionable target associated with androgen receptor-mediated therapy resistance. These observations were validated using a novel inhibitor of CBP/EP300, pocenbrodib, which showed preclinical activity in vitro and in vivo. Acetylomics analysis and functional studies pinpointed inhibition of oxidative phosphorylation and fatty acid metabolism as key mechanisms of action for pocenbrodib. Clinical benefit for this agent was demonstrated in a patient with metastatic APM-resistant prostate cancer (NCT04575766), highlighting CBP/EP300 as a key target for further translation.

after.title: Preprint: Long-read sequencing resolves functional CYP2D6 alleles tagged by a cocaine use disorder associated haplotype
after.authors: Garvin, M. R.; Rosenblum, D. M.; Bergen, A. W.; Weiss, S. H.
after.abstract: The CYP2D6 locus exhibits extensive allelic diversity and structural complexity, complicating the identification of functional variants underlying genetic associations. We previously identified a four-single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) haplotype (AACG) associated with cocaine use disorder and altered CYP2D6 expression in the brain. To characterize the molecular variation of this haplotype, we performed targeted PacBio long-read sequencing on 19 individuals of European ancestry carrying zero, one, or two copies of AACG. Complementary analyses included human pangenome assemblies, protein structural modeling, splice quantitative trait loci, and SNP-array probe sequences. Long-read sequencing resolved distinct CYP2D6 alleles associated with AACG, including CYP2D6 star 2 and star 4. Four of five individuals lacking AACG carried two canonical reference alleles, whereas nearly all AACG homozygotes carried noncanonical alleles. The star 2 allele contained two missense substitutions (R296C and S486T), while star 4 carried four missense substitutions (P34S, L91M, H94R, and S486T) and a loss-of-function splice-site mutation. Structural comparisons suggested potential substrate-dependent effects on ligand binding, while publicly available transcriptomic data associated AACG variants with altered splice-junction usage across multiple tissues, including brain. Although SNP-array intensity differences initially suggested copy-number variation, long-read sequencing did not support consistent gene dosage differences. Instead, polymorphisms within array probe-binding regions provided a plausible explanation for these signals. These findings demonstrate that a disease-associated SNP haplotype tags functionally distinct CYP2D6 alleles and highlight the importance of haplotype-resolved sequencing for interpreting genetic associations at complex pharmacogenomic loci.

after.title: Preprint: Eating disorder phenotypes differ in their genetic relationships with impulsivity facets
after.authors: Vilar Ribo, L.; Digiulio, R.; Bianchi, S.; Choi, M.; Gustavson, D.; Sanchez-Roige, S.
after.abstract: Background. Eating disorders are clinically heterogeneous and characterized by distinct patterns of control over food intake. Anorexia nervosa (AN) is characterized by excessive dietary restraint, whereas binge-eating (BE) is a transdiagnostic behavior defined by loss of control over eating. Understanding the relationship between eating disorders and impulsivity may provide insights into their underlying mechanisms and identify potential targets for prevention and treatment. Methods. We used genome-wide association study data (N=82,707-1,268,116) and genomic structural equation modeling to examine genetic relationships between eating disorder phenotypes (AN, ANRestrictive, ANBinge-Purging, and BE) and impulsivity facets (five UPPS-P, three BIS-11, and delay discounting). We examined whether these relationships persisted after conditioning on the genetic liability for substance use disorders (SUDs) and body mass index (BMI). Results. AN and its subtypes showed negative genetic correlations with delay discounting, the magnitude of this correlation being stronger for ANRestrictive. ANRestrictive also showed negative genetic correlations with sensation seeking and common impulsivity, whereas ANBinge-Purging showed a positive genetic correlation with urgency-specific impulsivity. In contrast, BE showed positive genetic correlations with both common and urgency-specific impulsivity. Several associations remained significant after controlling for SUDs and BMI, including the negative association between AN with delay discounting, the negative associations with AN and ANRestrictive with sensation seeking, and the positive association between BE and urgency-specific impulsivity. Conclusion. These findings reveal complex patterns of genetic overlap between eating disorder phenotypes and impulsivity dimensions. Understanding these phenotype-specific relationships may help explain clinical heterogeneity and inform the development of more targeted prevention and treatment strategies.

This simulation study aims to quantify this effect using setting parameters based on cardiovascular disease prediction and intervention and assess if including a treatment variable in…

data.summary: added: Preprint: Effect of a feedback loop on clinical prediction model performance

after.title: Preprint: Effect of a feedback loop on clinical prediction model performance
after.authors: Pacynko, S.; Sperrin, M.; Jenkins, D.
after.abstract: Clinical prediction models (CPMs) that guide treatment-initiation, and therefore affect patient outcomes, may create feedback loops when updated using data from patients whose care they influenced. Treatment can alter predictor-outcome relationships and outcome prevalence, potentially reducing model performance. This simulation study aims to quantify this effect using setting parameters based on cardiovascular disease prediction and intervention and assess if including a treatment variable in the model mitigates any performance degradation. In the simulation, models were developed to predict the probability of a binary adverse outcome, guide treatment allocation, and then updated using data containing patients in whom the model was applied. Scenarios varied treatment inclusion as a predictor in the model and the presence of unmeasured confounding. Performance was assessed with calibration-in-the-large, calibration slope, c-statistic, and correct risk assignment relative to treatment threshold. Without unmeasured confounding, excluding treatment as a predictor resulted in miscalibration, but including treatment solves this problem completely. With unmeasured confounding, performance deteriorated even when treatment was included. These results agree with previous findings and illustrate the likelihood that models that guide interventions may experience performance deterioration due to the difficulty of recording treatment and avoiding unmeasured confounders. Causal inference methods combined with risk prediction may help address this problem. Further research is needed on monitoring techniques to allow detection of this issue post-model implementation.

after.authors: Mann, S.; Berdahl, C. T.; Griffin, B. A.
after.abstract: Rossetti et al. report that hospitalized patients whose care was informed by an AI-based clinical deterioration early warning system (EWS) were 36% less likely to die during a pragmatic cluster-randomized trial when compared to patients on usual care units without the EWS (adjusted hazard ratio [HR], 0.64; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.53-0.78).1 The authors should be applauded for conducting a trial evaluating the effect of an AI intervention on patient health outcomes; more such trials are needed. Several aspects of the study, however, raise concerns that its findings may not accurately reflect the effect of the EWS. First, spillover effects on availability of scarce intensive care unit (ICU) beds could have led to worse outcomes for patients in the control group. Second, EWS-informed clinical decisions may have led to more frequent exclusion of high-risk patients from the intervention group. Either of these concerns could have led to overestimation of AI benefit. Finally, large pre-trial differences in hospital unit mortality rates suggest that unreported cluster-level imbalance or between-cluster variance could also have affected trial results.

data.summary: added: Preprint: Optimizing Sepsis Treatment via Latent Protocol Inference

after.title: Preprint: Optimizing Sepsis Treatment via Latent Protocol Inference
after.authors: Wang, C.; Liu, V.; Honig, E.; Kong, D.; Wu, Y. N.
after.abstract: Sepsis is a life-threatening medical emergency characterized by high mortality and variable treatment practices. Optimizing treatment from retrospective data is challenging due to sparse, delayed outcomes and complex physiological dynamics. We introduce the Generative Latent Protocol Model (GLPM), a probabilistic framework that structures clinical decision-making through a latent protocol variable anchored on the patient's admission state. This latent variable acts as an information bottleneck, decoupling the generation of treatment trajectories from the prediction of survival outcomes. Unlike methods that rely on value estimation or noisy return-to-go conditioning, our model is trained via maximum likelihood estimation to capture the joint distribution of treatment trajectories and outcomes. At inference time, we treat treatment optimization as a probabilistic inverse problem: we sample latent protocols from a posterior distribution conditioned on a target survival probability. On the ICU-Sepsis benchmark derived from MIMIC-III, our best variant matches or exceeds eight offline baselines on all five datasets, with gains that are statistically significant against every baseline on the most heterogeneous dataset, and offers interpretability through patient-specific counterfactual analysis.

after.authors: Sambore, D.; Meksem, L.; Huang, F.; Godet, J.
after.abstract: Objectives: Online reviews constitute a source of information on the experience of users in community pharmacies. The way in which pharmacists engage with them remains poorly documented. The objective was to describe the frequency, determinants, and content of the responses provided by French pharmacy teams to reviews published on Google Maps. Methods: Cross-sectional observational study. Public reviews from nearly all French community pharmacies (approximately 20 000) were collected automatically between September and October 2026. For each review, the rating, the text of the review, the time since its publication, and the text of the response, if it existed, were collected. Factors associated with the response were studied using logistic regression. Sentiment of the reviews and the tone of the responses were automatically coded according to a predefined grid. The presence of reviews generated by artificial intelligence, as well as potential interventions on the ratings, were explored.\newline Results: In total, 1 008 024 extractions (729 521 reviews and 278 504 responses) concerning 19 985 pharmacies were analysed. A response was present for 38% of reviews and 67.5% of pharmacies had responded at least once. after.authors: Potka, S.; Mugabo, H.; Rehman, R. U.; Liu, A.; Manson, M.; Tuyisenge, J.; Semakula, M.; Lester, R.
after.abstract: Background Linguistic barriers between patients and providers cause diagnostic error, poor adherence, and adverse events, and disproportionately affect speakers of low-resource languages. Kinyarwanda, spoken by more than 20 million people, has a small digital footprint, and the quality of off-the-shelf machine translation (MT) for its clinical dialogue is poorly documented. Methods We evaluated six MT systems (GPT-5, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Azure Translate, Google Translate, and NLLB-200) for Kinyarwanda-to-English patient-provider conversations. Using a professional reference corpus of 600 conversations, stratified across three pandemic periods and collected in Rwanda via the WelTel platform, we assessed automated metrics (semantic similarity, BLEU, chrF, and translation edit rate [TER]) and 0-100 quality ratings from three professional Kinyarwanda-English translators, with reliability quantified by intraclass correlation (ICC). De-identified secondary data were approved by UBC (H20-01031) and the Rwanda National Ethics Committee (100/RNEC/2020). Findings On the full 600-conversation cohort, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-5, and Gemini 2.5 Flash had closely clustered semantic similarity (0.877, 0.874, 0.873), well above Azure Translate (0.809) and NLLB-200 (0.754); Gemini 2.5 Flash led on BLEU (43.13) and the lowest TER (68.15). Translators ranked GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Flash highest (means 81.55 and 81.51), then GPT-4o-mini (72.67), Azure Translate (55.16), and NLLB-200 (39.05); average-rater reliability was moderate (ICC 0.594, rising to 0.701 on a balanced 85-conversation subset). Automated n-gram metrics understated the quality gap human raters perceived between large language models and conventional systems. Interpretation GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Flash are the strongest off-the-shelf systems for Kinyarwanda-English clinical translation and primary choices for human-in-the-loop use, with GPT-4o-mini a cost-efficient alternative. NLLB-200 underperformed, showing that models built for low-resource languages are not automatically suited to specialised clinical domains without fine-tuning. Human evaluation should be prioritised over automated metrics alone when comparing LLM-based translation.

after.title: Preprint: Leveraging HCUP Data to Predict Preventable Admissions in Patients with Chronic Kidney Diseases
after.authors: Huang, Y.-C.; Han, Y.; Liu, Y.-C.; Parikh, C.; Kharrazi, H.; Baughman, D.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Biomedical Informatics and Data Science, Johns Hopkins School of Medicine
after.abstract: Objectives: This study developed machine learning (ML) to predict 90-day preventable admissions in CKD patients while evaluating racial disparities in model performance. Materials and Methods: Study population included CKD patients (above 18 years) with hospital encounters in Maryland (2016-2023). Logistic regression (LR), random forest (RF), XGBoost, and k-nearest neighbors (KNN) models were used to predict 90-day preventable admissions after a CKD outpatient visit. Data used in this study was extracted from Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project (HCUP). Results: 28,214 unique patients were included, of whom 3974 (14%) experienced a subsequent preventable admission. LR achieved comparable performance with RF and XGBoost (AuROC 0.784 - 0.788, AuPRC 0.397 - 0.416), outperforming KNN (AuROC 0.753, AuPRC 0.342). All models performed marginally better in the Black population (AuROC 0.773 - 0.807, AuPRC 0.369 - 0.467) than in the white population (AuROC 0.738 - 0.776, AuPRC 0.329 - 0.394). The false negative rates (FNR) in the white population were higher across different models (Black: 0.236 - 0.33, white: 0.297 - 0.377). Discussion: Our results suggest that LR can achieve comparable prediction performances than tree-based ML algorithms. Hospital utilization and congestive heart failure are among the most important predictors across models. Further analyses on prediction bias revealed that FNRs are more significant in white patients, which can be due to their overall lower utilization. Conclusions: This study demonstrated a pipeline to develop ML models predicting preventable admissions while revealing existing racial biases. These findings can inform ambulatory settings on how to reduce preventable admissions among CKD patients.

after.abstract: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is associated with widespread multi-organ comorbidity, but these outcomes have never been quantified comprehensively against a population without hemoglobinopathies or hemolytic anemias. That gap limits clinical appreciation of the breadth of SCD-associated illness and, because burden-of-disease frameworks require exposure-outcome effect sizes, it also leaves SCD systematically under-counted in global health estimates. Using longitudinal utilization and demographic data from MarketScan for 2016 to 2019, we fitted Bayesian meta-regressions of comparative rates of 30 acute and chronic diseases among individuals with and without an SCD diagnosis, by age and sex. Individuals with SCD had elevated risk of nearly every outcome, with the highest relative risk (RR) and incidence rate ratio (IRR; per person-year) generally in the youngest age groups. This included well-established problems such as chronic pain (RR=12.0, 95% UI 11.0-13.0), but also conditions in which impaired perfusion or persistent vascular injury may be causal: preeclampsia (IRR=9.7, 7.8-12.1), postpartum hemorrhage (IRR=13.6, 11.2-16.1), pulmonary hypertension (RR=96.3, 85.9-108.1), acute myocardial infarction (IRR=28.7, 24.5-34.3), ischemic stroke (RR=16.7, 15.0-18.6), kidney disease (RR=11.9, 10.9-13.0), asthma (RR=3.21, 2.98-3.44) and lower respiratory infections (IRR=2.85, 2.69-3.02). These results supply the inputs needed to quantify indirect SCD burden in comparative risk assessment frameworks. These results establish SCD as a whole-body risk factor rather than a single-organ disease, which should inform treatment guidelines and population-level health programs in settings where SCD is endemic.

after.authors: Leung, T.; Stopard, I. J.; Wood, J. G.; Hogan, A. B.
after.abstract: Background: Seasonal influenza is a common cause of severe illness, particularly in young children and older adults. In Australia, influenza vaccination programs using the inactivated influenza vaccine (IIV) largely focus on direct protection of older adults. Live-attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) is now available for children aged 2-17 years, offering an opportunity to complement existing IIV programs. Methods: We developed a mathematical model of seasonal influenza transmission and vaccination in Australia, calibrated to surveillance data. We evaluated the health impact of LAIV programs on influenza burden relative to a baseline IIV-only scenario that assumed current coverage levels. We compared the dose efficiency of LAIV programs targeting school-aged children with strategies that increased IIV uptake in adults. Findings: An LAIV program targeting children aged 5-17 years was estimated to have the largest population-level impact, reducing influenza hospitalisations by 16% and deaths by 13%, assuming 55% coverage. An IIV program achieving 55% coverage in adults aged 50 years and older was predicted to have a similar population-level reduction in hospitalisations to a primary school-aged LAIV program (around 9.5%). Based only on doses administered, LAIV programs were more efficient at averting cases, hospitalisations, and deaths than strategies that expanded IIV uptake in adults. However, for outcomes in adults [≥]65 years old, increasing IIV uptake in this age group was estimated to be the most efficient strategy, with a number needed to vaccinate of 1811 to avert one hospitalisation. Interpretation: Our results support the potential use of LAIV as an additional tool in the prevention of seasonal influenza in Australia.

after.authors: NGASSAM KAMGNO, I.; MURHABAZI BASHOMBWA, A.; NANA DJAPOU, M. C.; BLAMA ABBA, I.; NGOUNOU NTONWEN, H. A.; BUH NKUM, C.; WANDJI NONO, A. V.; NGUEDIA DONGMO, I. W.; ATEUKENG, C. G.; ATEUDJIEU, J.
after.abstract: Background Limited access to quality emergency neonatal care (EmNC) contributes to high neonatal mortality in Cameroon, yet data on facility readiness in the West Region are scarce. This study assessed the preparedness of health facilities for EmNC in this region. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional study from March to May 2026 in five health districts of the West Region. All eligible facilities were included. Data were collected through a questionnaire for health professionals and an observation checklist adapted from the WHO/UNFPA SARA framework. Preparedness scores were classified as high ([≥]80%), moderate (60-79%) or low (<60%). Results We surveyed 185 health facilities (74.1% integrated health centers, 63.2% rural, 49.7% public) and 243 health professionals. The mean preparedness score was 51.1%; 11.4% of facilities had a high level of preparedness, 20.0% moderate and 68.6% low. At least one qualified staff member was present in 64.3% of facilities, and written neonatal protocols in 45.9%. Essential equipment was scarce: bag-valve-mask (13.0%), functional incubator (19.5%), newborn transport equipment (13.5%), phototherapy unit (10.8%) and defibrillator (7.6%), whereas vitamin K was widely available (95.7%). Mean scores were highest in private for-profit facilities (64.9%) compared with public (47.7%) and private non-profit facilities (45.1%), in district hospitals (66.2%) and CMAs (66.0%) compared with integrated health centers (45.9%), and in urban areas (60.9%) compared with rural (48.6%) and semi-urban areas (40.4%). Conclusions Most health facilities in the West Region are poorly prepared for newborn emergencies. Priorities include essential equipment with maintenance systems, qualified staff, written protocols and regular training, especially in integrated health centers and rural areas.

after.authors: Selby, R. R.; Liang, K.; Parina, R.; Livits, I.; Tran, G.; Nguyen, P.; Sher, L.; Korc, P.; Kankotia, R.; Breit, M.; Braxton, D. R.; Penisson, S.; Tomasetti, C.; Von Hoff, D. D.; Grossman, S. R.
after.abstract: Background Mucinous pancreatic cysts demonstrate malignant risk and expanding prevalence. Society guidelines lack underpinning from large, single-center experiences. We describe pancreatic mucinous cyst epidemiology, compare cyst-derived cancers from surveilled vs. non-surveilled cohorts, analyze risk metrics using surveillance and pathologic outcomes, and propose a weighted cancer risk probability score. Methods We conducted a retrospective study of patients at a tertiary metropolitan hospital between January 2006 and December 2025 who were found to have a mucinous pancreatic cyst or cyst-derived cancer on endoscopic ultrasound (EUS). A diagnostic algorithm was used to presumptively diagnose cyst phenotypes; diagnoses were clarified through surveillance and surgery. A preliminary risk classification scheme categorized patients to a risk level based on six binary variables. Cyst-derived cancer (CDCa) were categorized by first encounter or progression from surveillance. Survival analysis of surgical patients was organized by histologic grade and tumor stage. We developed a new malignant progression risk formula that weighted the four most predictive risk metrics: cyst size, main duct phenotype, pancreatic duct dilation, and bile duct dilation. Results 3667 cysts in 3643 patients were analyzed; 2087 (57%) were branch duct and 93 (2.9%) were main duct intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMN), and 79 (2.4%) were mucinous cystic neoplasms (MCN). Unclassifiable cysts (n = 1386, 32%) were analyzed as a primordial branch duct IPMN cohort due to volume and gender equivalents. IPMN-MD were often mislabeled as IPMN-BD during surveillance (43%). Our initial recommended surveillance interval was based on six unweighted metrics: solid nodule, pancreatic or bile duct dilation, main duct involvement, and fluid chemistry. Cyst-derived cancers developed in 8% of mucinous cysts (n = 162). Resection was performed in 184 patients from surveilled (n = 76) and non-surveilled (n = 108) cohorts. Surveilled patients had fewer advanced stage cancers; however, explant pathology was low/moderate dysplasia in 72 resected patients. Kaplan-Meier survival at 5 years was 82% with high-grade dysplasia and T1N0 and 50% for T2N0 and T3N0 lesions. Frequencies of malignant cyst progression were main duct IPMNs (53%), branch duct IPMN (6%), and MCN (5%). Mucinous cyst-derived cancers accounted for 10.7% of all pancreatic adenocarcinomas within our registry. Our logistic regression model achieved a cross-validated area under the ROC of 0.957 (95% CI: 0.944-0.968), with 90% sensitivity at a threshold corresponding to 90% specificity. Conclusion In this longitudinal cohort study, branch duct IPMN was the dominant phenotype, yet main duct IPMN was most likely to progress to malignancy. Surveillance favored early cancer diagnosis yet with low specificity. Post resection survival was excellent and explant pathology revealed lower frequency of nodal disease when compared to PDAC. Risk metric analysis led to a new risk-formulation strategy for patient selection. Our new weighted risk formula offers high predictive accuracy, helping to avoid unnecessary resections.

Cyst-derived cancers developed in 8% of mucinous cysts (n = 162). Resection was performed in 184 patients from surveilled (n = 76) and non-surveilled (n = 108) cohorts. Surveilled patients had fewer advanced stage cancers; however, explant pathology was low/moderate dysplasia in 72 resected patients. Kaplan-Meier survival at 5 years was 82% with high-grade dysplasia and T1N0 and 50% for T2N0 and T3N0 lesions. Frequencies of malignant cyst progression were main duct IPMNs (53%), branch duct IPMN (6%), and MCN (5%). Mucinous cyst-derived cancers accounted for 10.7% of all pancreatic adenocarcinomas within our registry. Our logistic regression model achieved a cross-validated area under the ROC of 0.957 (95% CI: 0.944-0.968), with 90% sensitivity at a threshold corresponding to 90% specificity. after.title: Preprint: Resilience following a nature-based retreat: a prospective observational study
after.authors: Balin, R.; Lev, M.; Schneider Moreh, A.; Grotto, I.
after.author_corresponding_institution: School of Public Health, Faculty of Health Sciences, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Beer-Sheva, Israel
after.abstract: Background: Residential nature-based programs may support resilience and well-being among people experiencing substantial psychological distress. We examined changes following an independently organized retreat. Methods: This prospective observational study followed 18 adults attending a five-day resilience retreat in Finland. The study did not undertake diagnostic assessments or assign retreat participation. The primary outcome was CD-RISC-10 resilience at 21 days after the retreat. Secondary outcomes included perceived stress, affect, well-being, self-efficacy and posttraumatic stress symptoms. Analyses used mixed-effects models and paired Wilcoxon tests. Results: At 21 days, the mixed model showed a 5.08-point increase in CD-RISC-10 (95% CI 2.51 to 7.65; p = 0.00011). The estimate persisted on a small-sample reference (p = 0.00034) and among the 14 participants with an intake reading (+4.59 points; p = 0.0014). Perceived stress, positive and negative affect, well-being and self-efficacy also registered improvement (each paired p < 0.01). Well-being rose by 21.66 points on the 0 to 100 WHO-5 index (95% Wald CI 14.29 to 29.03). Score improvements were largest at retreat completion, partly subsided by 14 days where measured but were sustained to the 21-day mark. Evidence for improvement in posttraumatic stress symptoms was less definitive. Limitations: Uncontrolled design and a small sample limit causal interpretation. Conclusions: Higher self-reported resilience and improved well-being persisted three weeks after the retreat. The findings support controlled evaluation of the program. Registration: Open Science Framework, DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/7WKM5.

after.title: Preprint: Community-Based Hypertension Screening in Urban and Rural Zimbabwe: A Comparative Analysis and Implementation Lessons (2022-2025)
after.authors: Chimberengwa, P. T.; Masiye, K.; Bepe, T. O.; Mhlanga, T. T.; Dhodho, E.; Chinyanga, T. T.
after.author_corresponding_institution: National University of Science and Technology
after.abstract: Introduction Hypertension is a leading cause of cardiovascular disease and a growing public health challenge in sub-Saharan Africa. Community-based screening delivered through community health workers (CHWs) may improve early detection and strengthen decentralized chronic disease services, particularly in underserved settings. This study compared hypertension screening yield across phased implementation of a community-based programme in urban and rural Zimbabwe and documented implementation lessons for decentralized hypertension services. Methods A retrospective comparative analysis was conducted using aggregate programme data routinely captured in the District Health Information System 2. Screening outcomes from Phase 1 (2022-2023) were compared with those from the combined Phase 2 and Phase 3 implementation period (2024-2025). Trained CHWs used digital blood pressure devices to screen adults in communities and outreach settings, refer individuals with elevated blood pressure to primary healthcare facilities, and support follow-up. Phase 1 was implemented in urban districts and targeted adults aged [≥]40 years, while subsequent phases expanded to adults aged [≥]18 years and predominantly rural and peri-urban populations. The primary outcome was hypertension screening positivity, while secondary outcomes included participant characteristics and age-specific positivity rates. Results A total of 410,568 adults were screened, including 120,144 urban adults aged [≥]40 years in Phase 1 and 290,424 adults in Phases 2 and 3. Among participants in Phases 2 and 3, 76.0% resided in rural communities, 64.9% were female, and 44.9% were living with HIV. Hypertension positivity was 41.0% (49,276/120,144; 95% CI 40.7%-41.3%) in Phase 1 and 14.5% (41,972/290,424; 95% CI 14.3%-14.6%) in Phases 2 and 3 (p<0.001). Positivity increased significantly with age in both periods, ranging from 31.8% to 51.6% in Phase 1 and from 13.5% to 28.4% in later phases (all p<0.001). Conclusion Community-based hypertension screening delivered by CHWs successfully reached large urban and rural populations and identified substantial hypertension burden, particularly among older adults. The lower positivity observed in later phases likely reflects differences in age eligibility and population mix rather than programme effect. Scaling CHW-led screening may strengthen decentralized hypertension detection, although nationally representative surveys and longitudinal studies are needed to assess linkage to care, treatment initiation, and long-term blood pressure control. Key Words Hypertension; Community health workers; Community-based screening; Primary healthcare; Decentralized care; Zimbabwe.

after.title: Preprint: Developing a Stakeholder-Driven One Health Collaboration Framework for Bovine Tuberculosis Control at the Human-Animal Interface in Lundazi and Monze Districts, Zambia
after.authors: Phiri, A.; Zulu, M.; Phiri, M.; NYIRENDA, W.; Phiri, E.; Olea-Popelka, F.; Malama, S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Zambia School of Veterinary Medicine
after.abstract: Background: Bovine tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium bovis, is a neglected zoonosis at the human-animal interface in Zambia, particularly affecting cattle-dependent rural communities in Eastern and Southern Provinces, where cattle are central to livelihoods, nutrition, and cultural identity. While Zambia has a One Health Strategic Plan 2022-2026 and a One Health Secretariat under Zambia National Public Health Institute, operational collaboration between veterinary and medical sectors at district level remains fragmented, contributing to diagnostic gaps, under-reporting, and continued transmission through consumption of raw milk, undercooked meat, and occupational exposure during slaughter and handling of infected carcasses. The disconnect between national policy and district implementation has created a vacuum where frontline workers operate in isolation despite sharing the same disease burden. Methods: This qualitative exploratory study was conducted in Lundazi District (Eastern Province) and Monze District (Southern Province), Zambia, from February to June 2022. Ten Focus Group Discussions were conducted with 104 participants, including cattle farmers, cattle businessmen, abattoir workers, veterinary and para-veterinary professionals, and medical doctors, and ten Key Informant Interviews were conducted with District Veterinary Officers, District Medical Officers, Ministry of Health officials, and Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock officials. Participants were purposively selected based on their role, experience, and knowledge of bovine tuberculosis and One Health collaboration. Discussions were held in local languages (Tumbuka, Tonga, Chewa), audio-recorded with consent, transcribed verbatim, translated into English, and imported into NVivo 12 (QSR International, Melbourne, Australia) for thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke's six-step approach, with framework matrices for triangulation and trustworthiness. This methodological rigor ensured that diverse voices from community to policy level were systematically captured and compared. Results: Five themes emerged: (1) awareness of bovine tuberculosis, (2) socio-economic impacts, (3) public health impacts, (4) cultural practices and transmission, and (5) collaboration gaps and proposed framework. Medical and veterinary professionals demonstrated excellent awareness, while cattle farmers and abattoir workers showed poor awareness. Socio-economic impacts included reduced milk yield and carcass condemnation. Key barriers to collaboration included lack of diagnostic capacity at district hospitals to differentiate Mycobacterium bovis from Mycobacterium tuberculosis, siloed training curricula, absence of formal round-table coordination mechanisms, and limited funding. An existing enabler was informal collaboration in meat inspection between veterinary assistants and environmental health officers. Based on these findings, a five-pillar One Health Collaboration Framework is proposed. This framework was co-constructed from participant recommendations, making it contextually grounded and acceptable to end-users. Conclusion: Effective control of bovine tuberculosis in Zambia requires institutionalized One Health collaboration, moving from informal ad hoc interactions to formal governance structures. The proposed framework provides a practical, low-cost and contextually grounded roadmap for district-level implementation and is applicable to other zoonoses such as brucellosis, anthrax and rabies. Its implementation can help break the cycle of under-reporting and under-funding that currently sustains zoonotic transmission in rural Zambia

after.authors: AlAmmar, H.; Chowdhary, I.; Shaikh, A. G.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Louis Stokes Cleveland VA Medical Center, University Hospitals, Case Western Reserve University
after.abstract: Oculopalatal tremor (OPT) follows disruption of the cerebello-rubro-olivary network and is frequently associated with hypertrophic inferior-olive degeneration (HOD). HOD does not invariably produce OPT; determinants of oculo-palatal, ocular-only, palatal-only, or non-oscillatory phenotypes remain undefined. We analyzed 501 patients with HOD, of which 424 with classifiable laterality: 52.1% had unilateral and 47.9% bilateral HOD. Lesion location predicted HOD laterality (chi-square=35.65, p=3.4x10^-7; Cramer V=0.31): brainstem/pons lesions produced ipsilateral HOD in 70.0%, whereas cerebellar lesions produced contralateral HOD in 86.4%. Bilateral HOD reflected combined cerebellar/brainstem lesions, and was associated with ocular oscillations (OR 2.66, 95% CI 1.31-5.43; p=0.0067) but not convincingly palatal oscillations (OR 1.49, 95% CI 0.91-2.42; p=0.137). Phenotype differed by etiology (p=0.0024): hemorrhagic and vascular-malformation lesions preferentially produced combined OPT, ischemic lesions were enriched among ocular-only presentations, and neoplastic lesions produced the most heterogeneous phenotype and were disproportionately represented among palatal-only cases. Age, sex, and lesion laterality were not associated with phenotype. Four-class prediction was limited (macro AUC 0.555; balanced accuracy 0.301), with little improvement after adding HOD laterality (macro AUC 0.563; balanced accuracy 0.323). Among classifiable OPT waveforms, 96.9% contained a pendular component. Median OPT latency was 6 months (IQR 4.75-24); lesion location, etiology, and HOD laterality did not predict latency. HOD is therefore an important substrate, but lesion anatomy and etiology shape group-level phenotype without enabling reliable individual prediction.

after.authors: langley, j.; Hwang, K. S.; Hu, X. P.
after.abstract: Background: Lewy body (LB) copathology in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is associated with earlier symptom onset and faster cognitive decline. Depigmentation of substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) volume is seen in both Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies. We examined whether lower antemortem SNc volume was associated with autopsy confirmed LB pathology in patients with AD or mild cognitive impairment (MCI). Methods: Seventy-three participants with a clinical diagnosis of AD or MCI, neuromelanin-sensitive MRI, and subsequent neuropathologic assessment from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative were studied. At autopsy, 33 participants had LB pathology (LB+) and 40 had no LB pathology (LB-). We compared SNc volume between groups using analysis of covariance adjusted for age and sex. Within the LB+ group, we assessed the association between SNc volume and nigral hypopigmentation using Spearman correlation. In a secondary analysis, we tested whether adding SNc volume to a logistic regression mode containing age, sex, and executive function improved model fit for autopsy-defined LB status. Results: LB+ participants had greater nigral hypopigmentation at autopsy and lower antemortem SNc volume than LB- participants. The adjusted mean difference in SNc volume (LB+ minus LB-) was -66 mm3 (95% confidence interval -115.9 to -16.2, P=0.010). Within the LB+ group, lower SNc volume was associated with greater hypopigmentation (Spearman rho;=-0.373, P=0.032). Among 71 participants with complete model data, adding SNc volume improved model fit (likelihood ratio=8.67, P=0.003). The combined model had an in sample area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.770 (95% confidence interval: 0.661-0.879). Conclusion: The correspondence between lower antemortem SNc volume and greater hypopigmentation at autopsy supports the use of neuromelanin-sensitive MRI to characterize nigral involvement in AD or MCI with LB copathology. These findings are based on a single cohort, and the interval of several years between imaging and autopsy limits how closely the pigmentation ratings reflect nigral integrity at imaging.

after.title: Preprint: Dynamic Macro-Microvascular Coupling During Cerebrovascular Reactivity Revealed by Simultaneous TCD and DCS
after.authors: Ji, Z.; Su, H.; Wang, Y.; Han, Y.-Q.; Li, Z.; Cao, X.
after.abstract: Background Transcranial Doppler (TCD) measures flow velocity in large intracranial arteries but provides limited information on microvascular perfusion.Diffuse correlation spectroscopy (DCS) enables continuous, noninvasive assessment of cortical microvascular blood flow. We compared macrovascular and microvascular responses during cerebrovascular reactivity testing. Methods Forty-four healthy adults (28 men; mean age, 27.0{+/-}3.8 years) underwent simultaneous bilateral TCD and DCS during a breath-holding task (1-minute baseline, 30-second breath hold, and 1-minute recovery). Middle cerebral artery flow velocity and cortical microvascular blood flow index were normalized to baseline (rCBFv and rCBFi, respectively). Temporal responses were compared using Pearson correlation and Bland-Altman analyses. Response amplitude, rise time, and recovery time were also assessed. Results TCD and DCS showed concordant response trajectories during breath holding and recovery. Correlations between normalized temporal responses were strong in both hemispheres (left,r=0.988{+/-}0.009;right, r=0.990{+/-}0.008; both P<0.001). Bland-Altman analysis showed minimal systematic bias and no proportional bias. No significant interhemispheric differences were observed in response amplitude, rise time, or recovery time. DCS-derived rCBFi showed greater response amplitudes and variability than TCD-derived rCBFv (left, 1.80{+/-}0.34 vs 1.63{+/-}0.15; right, 1.72{+/-}0.27 vs 1.63{+/-}0.14). Parameter-level analyses showed strong correlations and minimal bias for response amplitude, rise time, and recovery time. Conclusions TCD and DCS demonstrated strong temporal coupling during cerebrovascular reactivity testing, while DCS detected larger response amplitudes than TCD. These findings suggest that macrovascular velocity and cortical microvascular perfusion provide complementary information about cerebrovascular responses.

after.abstract: Pathogenic variants that increase LRRK2 kinase activity are a common genetic cause of Parkinson's disease. Most pathogenic variants occur within the catalytic ROC-COR GTPase (e.g. R1441C) and kinase (e.g. G2019S) domains, where they activate LRRK2 through distinct mechanisms. The common kinase-domain variant directly enhances the intrinsic catalytic activity of LRRK2, whereas ROC-COR variants shift the equilibrium towards its active conformation. Whether variants in the N-terminal armadillo (ARM) domain, which contains Rab GTPase-binding sites involved in LRRK2 membrane recruitment, activate LRRK2 through a different mechanism remains unclear. Here, we characterise the LRRK2 Madrid haplotype, comprising two ARM variants (L119P/L488P) identified in a multigenerational family with PD. In cellular assays, L488P, but not L119P, increased LRRK2-mediated Rab10 phosphorylation approximately two-fold. Increased LRRK2 pathway activity was likewise observed in primary neutrophils and monocytes from variant carriers, including individuals with and without PD. Multiplexed parallel reaction monitoring (PRM) mass spectrometry in neutrophils further demonstrated coordinated increases in phosphorylation of six endogenous Rab substrates (Rab3, Rab8, Rab10, Rab12, Rab35 and Rab43), demonstrating concordant pathway activation in cellular models and primary human blood cells. Mechanistically, L488P lies adjacent to ARM Rab-binding site 1, and its activating effect was abolished by the site-1-disrupting L403E substitution, whereas activation by the ROC-domain variant R1441C was retained. We further investigated five rare ARM-domain variants identified through GP2 and independent genetic datasets, of which two, F470S and V483G, showed increased LRRK2 pathway activity in a site-1-dependent manner, while the remaining three showed no substantial activation. Together, these findings demonstrate that L488P-mediated pathway activation is recapitulated in human variant carriers and depends on an intact ARM Rab-binding site 1, identifying a mechanism of LRRK2 regulation distinct from that of classical catalytic-core variants.

after.authors: Chow, M.; Finton, N.; Singh, K.; Lekshmi, D.; Cordova, M.; Yen, E.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Woman, Mother + Baby (WoMB) Research Institute, Tufts Medical Center
after.abstract: Background: Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) regulates appetite through its effect on the hypothalamus, but this is understudied in neonates. Objective: To determine the molecular effects of maternal THC on hypothalamic/reward gene regulation, feeding, and growth in neonates. Methods: Saliva samples of THC-exposed (n=25) and age-matched non-exposed (n=25) neonates underwent transcriptomic analysis of cannabinoid receptors and hypothalamic/reward genes. We explored sex differences and exposure type (THC vs THC+opioids). Continuous data were analyzed with a Student's t-test and categorical data with a Chi-squared test. Results: THC exposure was associated with upregulation of CNR1, POMC (p<0.05), and DRD2 (p=0.06). THC exposure also trended with greater feeding amount and less weight loss in the first 3 days of life. Gene expression also differed by sex and exposure type. Conclusion: Maternal THC use is associated with changes in hypothalamic and reward genes, accompanied by feeding and weight effects.

after.authors: Bommarito, J.; Anderson, E.; Springer, L.; Zhang, Y.; Heggeness, M.
after.abstract: Pregnancy brings many women into regular contact with healthcare and creates opportunities to recognize conditions that need attention beyond childbirth. We asked whether chronic conditions, unrelated to pregnancy itself, first appear in health care records more often as women enter pregnancy and have increased contact with the health system. We matched 175,505 women admitted for delivery in 2023 to women in the same US claims cohort whose pregnancies began later and who were not pregnant at the time. We compared billed outpatient evaluation days and first records of chronic hypertension, non-gestational diabetes, and sickle cell trait. Outpatient evaluation days rose after pregnancy began, while they changed little in the comparison group. Before 20 weeks of gestation, there were 2.4 additional first hypertension records per 1,000 women entering pregnancy (95% confidence interval 1.6 to 3.1). The difference was smaller for diabetes and much larger for sickle cell trait. We show that pregnancy is a window for bringing existing conditions into the claims record.

after.title: Preprint: Tabular Foundation AI Models in Healthcare: A WHO-Inspired Benchmark for Responsible AI and Trustworthiness
after.authors: Hasan, K. S.; Borsha, M. A. A.; Ritu, R. J.; Shabbir, L.
after.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are increasingly used for structured prediction, yet their suitability for healthcare applications remains uncertain because predictive performance alone does not establish fairness, probabilistic reliability, or robustness. We developed a multidimensional benchmark to compare four TFMs: TabFM, TabPFN, TabDPT, and TabICL, against Logistic Regression and XGBoost across a curated, standardized suite of ten WHO-aligned healthcare classification datasets across diverse disease domains. Additionally, we harmonized clinical schemas, standardized protected sex attributes and outcome targets, and released both balanced-scale and natural-prevalence variants of the datasets to establish a benchmarking resource in healthcare machine learning. All models were evaluated using identical five-fold stratified cross-validation partitions and standardized preprocessing. Performance was assessed using 20 metrics spanning predictive discrimination, sex-based fairness, probability calibration, and robustness to Gaussian feature perturbations. A composite Clinical Model Evaluation Score (CMES) was used to summarize performance across these dimensions. Google TabFM achieved the highest mean CMES (0.8811), followed closely by TabDPT (0.8796), TabICL (0.8775), TabPFN (0.8756), XGBoost (0.8650), and Logistic Regression (0.8549). The Friedman test indicated significant differences among models ({chi}2F (5) = 24.914, p = 1.45 x 10^-4; Kendalls W = 0.498). However, post-hoc comparisons revealed no statistically significant differences among the four TFMs after Holm correction. TFMs generally demonstrated stronger discrimination and probabilistic calibration than conventional baselines, with TabFM achieving the highest mean Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (0.9327) and the lowest expected calibration error (0.0674). Conversely, Logistic Regression exhibited the greatest stability under feature perturbations, while fairness performance varied substantially across datasets and models. These findings highlight the potential of TFMs for small-data healthcare prediction while demonstrating that their advantages are dimension-dependent. Multidimensional, dataset-specific evaluation and external validation remain essential before clinical implementation. All analysis codes, original datasets, and multiple variants of benchmark datasets are publicly available in a GitHub repository to ensure reproducibility and future research.

after.authors: Lydon, E.; Sax, P. K.; Van Phan, H.; Osborne, C.; Maddux, A. B.; Leroue, M. K.; Yehya, N.; Gunn-Sandell, L.; Zinter, M. S.; DeRisi, J. L.; Wagner, B.; Ambroggio, L.; Mourani, P. M.; Langelier, C. R.
after.abstract: Lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) is a leading cause of acute respiratory illness, yet distinguishing it from noninfectious conditions remains a clinical challenge. Measuring the host immune response in the blood or lower airways, rather than exclusively detecting pathogens, has emerged as an alternative diagnostic strategy. However, it remains unclear whether RNA or protein measurements yield greater diagnostic information, or whether the two capture the same underlying biology. To address this, we performed paired transcriptomics and proteomics on tracheal aspirate specimens from 105 critically ill children with respiratory failure, 72 with microbiologically confirmed LRTI and 33 with noninfectious causes. Both approaches detected a clear host signature of LRTI which converged on similar core immune pathways including interferon signaling, inflammation, and complement activation. Despite this, agreement between individual genes and their corresponding proteins was largely poor. Diagnostic classifiers built from either RNA or protein data identified LRTI with similarly high accuracy (AUC>0.90), but selected different top biomarkers, and yielded discordant classifications for 12% of patients. Taken together, we find that lower airway transcriptomics and proteomics capture similar global biological features of LRTI despite poor correlation between gene and protein expression, providing fresh insight into approaches for biomarker discovery and clinical translation.

after.title: Preprint: Automated CTA-Based Assessment of Aortic Remodeling Through Volumetric Biomarkers in Type B Aortic Dissection
after.authors: Maccarini, A.; Ferraresi, M.; Molinari, A.; Jovanovic, J.; Rossi, G.; Mainardi, L.; Cerveri, P.
after.abstract: Type B aortic dissection (TBAD) requires lifelong morphological monitoring using computed tomography angiography (CTA). TBAD separates blood flow into the true lumen (TL), the original aortic channel, and the false lumen (FL), created by the dissection. Although three-dimensional volumetric analysis may complement diameter-based surveillance, its clinical adoption is limited by the time required for manual segmentation, particularly in postoperative scans affected by metallic artifacts. This study developed and evaluated an automated CTA-based framework for volumetric surveillance of TBAD across native and post-TEVAR conditions. We propose AORTA-SCAN, a hierarchical multi-stage framework for automated segmentation of the aorta, TL, and FL, extended to stented anatomy through a metal-aware triple-input strategy. The system computes conventional diameter measurements and volumetric biomarkers, including the perfusion dissection index (PDI), defined as the ratio between perfused FL volume and total perfused aortic volume. Domain adaptation was achieved using transfer learning and partial-label learning across heterogeneous clinical annotations. In native cases, AORTA-SCAN achieved a global Dice score of 0.84 and significantly improved FL segmentation compared with the nnU-Net baseline (0.84 vs 0.71, p < 0.001). Volumetric analysis showed high agreement with expert references, with a mean PDI bias of -0.17%. In postoperative cases, TL segmentation remained robust (Dice = 0.90), while FL and stent Dice were 0.75 and 0.72, respectively. Processing was completed in less than 1 minute per case on a standard workstation. AORTA-SCAN enables automated volumetric surveillance of TBAD and supports scalable extraction of PDI and diameter biomarkers from native and post-TEVAR CTA.

after.authors: Clumeck, S.; Rojas, C. R.; Kowuor, D.; Sesay, H. S.; Ameh, S.; Galarraga, O.; Ogbuanu, I. U.
after.author_corresponding_institution: The Africa Research Collaborative (The ARC), on behalf of the Child Health and Mortality Prevention Surveillance
after.abstract: Objective. Developing equitable prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) policies requires local evidence, yet how socioeconomic, geographic, and health system factors jointly drive HIV-related child mortality remains underexplored in Sierra Leone. This study evaluated the association between socioeconomic status (SES), geographic access, and pediatric HIV-related mortality, while examining the system-level and sociocultural barriers driving missed PMTCT opportunities. Materials and Methods: We used a mixed-methods design. Quantitative analyses drew on Child Health and Mortality Prevention Surveillance Sierra Leone surveillance data (2019-2024) for deceased under five years old (U5s) with confirmed HIV status. Stepwise logistic regression evaluated associations between covariates (SES, maternal education, distance to health facilities) and a composite binary outcome of HIV-related death. Qualitatively, 33 key informant interviews with PMTCT stakeholders were analyzed using thematic framework analysis in Dedoose. Results: The quantitative sample included 1,230 deceased children, of whom 162 (13.2%) reported an HIV-related death. Maternal education and distance to health facilities were statistically significant predictors of HIV-related death, whereas wealth quintiles showed no association. The qualitative findings identified system-level constraints disrupting the PMTCT cascade, including delayed entry into antenatal care, weak postnatal follow-up, stockouts of HIV test kits and antiretroviral drugs, limited polymerase chain reaction capacity and delayed results, and gaps in scheduling, tracking, and data systems. Donor-driven targets and funding constraints shaped procurement and service availability. Stigma, fear of disclosure, confidentiality concerns, transport costs, and poverty further undermined engagement and retention. Conclusions: Pediatric HIV infection and related outcomes were driven by cumulative barriers across access, service readiness, and sociocultural context rather than household wealth alone. Improving PMTCT outcomes requires strengthening diagnostic and supply chain infrastructure, enhancing patient-tracking systems, and delivering stigma-sensitive, community-anchored care.

after.authors: Hong, S. G.; Ko, A.; Kim, D.; Ku, H.; Oh, J.-I.; Lee, J.; Lee, H.; Han, S. S.; Kim, Y.; Kwon, J.; Lee, J.; Lee, J. P.; Park, J. I.; Park, J. T.; An, J. N.; Moon, K.-C.; Kim, H. J.; Kim, Y.-G.; Park, S.; Kim, D. K.; KORNERSTONE investigators,
after.abstract: Background: Proteinuria, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and hematuria guide the care of IgA nephropathy, but hematuria has been less consistently associated with outcome than proteinuria, and whether these measurements reflect the same tissue process is unclear. Methods: Single-cell-level spatial transcriptomics (Xenium, 5,101 targets) profiled 3.08 million cells in biopsies from 60 patients with IgA nephropathy, followed for a median of 8.3 years, and 24 living kidney donors. Injury scores, the proportion of injured glomeruli and glomerular signaling were related to the clinical measurements, to injury in surrounding tubules and to confirmed 40% eGFR decline or kidney failure. after.authors: Belihu, K. D.; Iverson, K.; Ambus, T. Y.; Belhu, K. D.; Bejiga, B. Z.; Adel, M. A.; Goshu, N. G.; Zewde, B. M.; Beyene, T. F.; Biccard, B.; Belachew, F. K.
after.abstract: Abstract Background: Sustainable implementation of perioperative quality registries in low- and middle-income countries requires more than technical infrastructure; it also requires informed stakeholders, supportive attitudes, and embedded practice. Ethiopia's National Perioperative Quality Improvement Network (NaPQIN), established across 10 hospitals, provided an opportunity to examine whether structured community engagement and involvement (CEI) could improve knowledge, attitudes, and practices among healthcare stakeholders. Methods and findings: We conducted a convergent parallel mixed-methods study from July 2024 to December 2025 across 10 NaPQIN hospitals in Ethiopia. Pre-intervention (n=25) and post-intervention (n=18) KAP surveys were administered around a three-month CEI program that included training, information materials, workshops, supervision, and stakeholder engagement. Semi-structured interviews (n=14) provided qualitative context. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively, qualitative data were analyzed thematically, and findings were integrated through triangulation. Knowledge improved across most domains, with the largest gains in identifying the primary purposes of a surgical registry (+12.0 percentage points) and non-characteristics of a registry (+10.4 percentage points). Attitudes improved across all measured domains, with the largest gains in overall satisfaction with NaPQIN (+0.60 on a 5-point scale), perceived CEI contribution to NaPQIN sustainability (+0.59), and the importance of community engagement (+0.44). Practices improved more modestly: clinician daily registry use increased by 21.3 percentage points and institutional CEI formalization by 20.4 percentage points, whereas benchmarking use declined by 8.9 percentage points. Qualitative findings highlighted the value of perioperative data, persistent implementation barriers, and practical strategies for strengthening registry use in low-resource settings. Conclusions: CEI was associated with improved stakeholder knowledge and attitudes toward NaPQIN, with early signs of practice integration. These findings suggest that CEI may be an important component of perioperative quality improvement networks in low- and middle-income country settings, while also highlighting ongoing needs in workflow support, benchmarking capacity, and digital infrastructure.

after.title: Preprint: Age-Dependent Association of Tumor Mutational Burden With Overall Survival in Patients With Melanoma
after.authors: Lyu, Z.; Lian, C.; Zhou, L.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School
after.abstract: Importance: Estimates of the association of tumor mutational burden (TMB) with overall survival in melanoma come largely from pan-cancer subgroups or immunotherapy-restricted cohorts, and whether host factors modify TMB's prognostic value is unclear. Objective: To determine whether TMB is independently associated with overall survival in a clinically sequenced melanoma cohort, and whether patient age modifies that association. Design: This retrospective, single-institution cohort study ascertained vital status through the National Death Index, Massachusetts death records, and electronic health records, with follow-up through September 7, 2025. Data were analyzed from April to November 2026. Setting: A US academic health system. Participants: Patients with a cancer registry-confirmed melanoma diagnosis whose tumor tissue, collected from January 2012 to May 2024, was sequenced on a clinically implemented targeted next-generation sequencing panel (OncoPanel). Exposures: TMB, analyzed continuously (per doubling) and dichotomized at the 10 mutations/megabase threshold ("TMB-high"). Main Outcomes and Measures: The primary outcome was overall survival from the date of genomic specimen collection (sequencing); secondary outcomes were overall survival from diagnosis and melanoma-specific survival. Results: A total of 1063 patients (635 [59.7%] male; 1027 [96.6%] White; median age at sequencing, 65.6 years [IQR, 56.1-74.0]) were included; 445 (41.9%) died. TMB-high status was associated with better overall survival after adjustment for age, sex, and noncutaneous subtype (hazard ratio [HR], 0.63; 95% CI, 0.51-0.79). Median overall survival was 10.2 vs 4.8 years for TMB-high vs TMB-low patients (log-rank P < .001). Each doubling of TMB was associated with an adjusted HR of 0.80 (95% CI, 0.73-0.87), with no evidence of nonlinearity (P = .31). The association weakened with increasing age (interaction HR per decade, 1.29; 95% CI, 1.11-1.50; P < .001); the adjusted TMB-high HR was 0.46 (95% CI, 0.25-0.83) at age 40 years and 0.84 (95% CI, 0.61-1.17) at 80 years. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) were received by 823 (77.4%) patients. Conclusions and Relevance: In this cohort study, TMB from clinically implemented, targeted next-generation sequencing panels was associated with overall survival as a continuous gradient, and the association weakened with increasing age. Because most patients received ICIs, prognostic and predictive contributions could not be separated.

after.authors: Thindwa, D.; Mlongoti, L.; Mitole, N.; Kusakala, A.; Khwiya, M.; Kayembe, T.; Lisimba, E.; Phiri, J. A.; Sibale, L. L.; Jambo, K. C.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Health Data Science, University of Liverpool, Liverpool, UK
after.abstract: Despite longstanding infant pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13), residual vaccine-type (VT) carriage persists in Malawi, where human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) prevalence is high. Adults living with HIV (ALWH) on long-term (>1 year) antiretroviral therapy (ART) show higher pneumococcal carriage and shedding than HIV-uninfected adults, but their contribution to VT transmission remains unclear. We conducted a longitudinal household study in Malawi with weekly nasopharyngeal sampling and fitted a household transmission dynamic model using Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. We collected 906 samples from 302 participants: younger children (0-5 years), older children (6-17 years) and adults (18+ years) stratified by HIV status and ART duration. VT transmission was more intense with household mixing, with ALWH on long-term ART contributing most to onward transmission to younger children. In contrast, non-vaccine serotype (NVT) transmission was driven mainly by younger children across multiple household pathways. Younger children and ALWH on long-term ART had prolonged carriage, which may have sustained household transmission. VT acquisition was driven mainly by household exposure, whereas NVT acquisition was balanced between household and community sources. Unvaccinated ALWH substantially contribute to household pneumococcal transmission, sustaining residual VT carriage. Optimal pneumococcal vaccination strategies targeting ALWH should be evaluated in high HIV prevalence low-income settings.

after.authors: Spivak, N. M.; Bishay, A. A. E. D.; Hopkins, A. R.; Swenson, A. J.; Haroon, J.; Hayden, A.; Collins, E.; Schafer, S. F.; London, E. D.; Lee, M. L.; Bystritsky, A.; Schafer, M. E.; Chou, T.; Caulfield, K. A.; Dougherty, D. D.; George, M. S.; Bookheimer, S. Y.; Monti, M. M.; Distler, M. G.
after.abstract: Objective: Transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS) enables noninvasive, spatially precise modulation of deep brain structures, including the amygdala, a key node in anxiety-related circuitry. We evaluated whether repeated right-amygdala tFUS improves symptoms in patients with treatment-resistant generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). Methods: In this multisite, double-blind, sham-controlled pilot trial, 31 adults with treatment-resistant GAD were randomized 1:1 to active or sham right-amygdala tFUS. Across three academic centers, participants received four sessions over one month and were followed for a month afterward. The primary endpoint was baseline-to-final-visit change in Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAM-A) score. Post hoc, subject-specific acoustic modeling assessed target engagement among active-treatment participants at UCLA. Results: tFUS delivered both in the scanner (visits 1,4) and out of the scanner (visits 2,3) was well tolerated with no worsening of anxiety. HAM-A scores decreased by 10.33 points (SD 9.51) with active tFUS and 8.81 points (SD 9.89) with sham, with no significant between-group difference (mean difference, -1.52; 95% CI, -8.65 to 5.61; p=.333; Cohens d=-0.16). HAM-A scores declined significantly over time across participants (p<.001), but trajectories did not differ between groups (p=.934). Acoustic modeling in four active participants demonstrated overlap of the simulated field with the right amygdala, although target coverage was limited and variable. Conclusions: Repeated right-amygdala tFUS was feasible for treatment-resistant GAD, but this small study found no significant clinical benefits over sham. Improvements in both groups, no differential physiological effects, and limited target coverage warrant adequately powered trials testing optimized dosing, precise targeting, and state-dependent or symptom-provocation paradigms.

after.authors: Xu, S.; Hill, J.; Cui, L.; He, P.; Feng, Y.; Jiang, N.; Niaura, R. S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Biostatistics, School of Global Public Health, New York University
after.abstract: Objective. Observational evidence on the effects of ENDS use on cigarette smoking cessation remains mixed, partly because of potential confounding. This study aimed to estimate the effects of ENDS use on subsequent current smoking over a two-year follow-up. Methods. We analyzed longitudinal data from Waves 4 to 6 of the Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health (PATH) Study (collected between 2016/12 and 2021/11), comprising a cohort of 4,792 US adults who were current established cigarette smokers at Wave 4. Using Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART) for causal inference, we estimated the effect of current ENDS use on subsequent current smoking, adjusting for a comprehensive set of 25 pre-exposure covariates. We characterized ENDS exposure as no use (0 days), some-day use (1 - 29 days), and daily use (30 days) in the past 30 days. Current cigarette smoking outcome was defined as past-30-day smoking, two years after the exposure measure. Results. Over a two-year period, daily ENDS use substantially reduced the percentage of current smoking compared with no use (estimate = -15.7%, 95% CI: -21.5% to -9.9%) or compared with some-day use (estimate = -15.0%, 95% CI: -22.3% to -7.8%). In contrast, some-day ENDS reduced a much smaller percentage compared with no use (estimate = -0.6%, 95% CI: -3.2% to -2.0%). Sensitivity analyses indicated that the estimated effect of daily ENDS use was robust to moderate-to-large unmeasured confounding. There was no evidence that these effects varied meaningfully by sex, race/ethnicity, annual household income, sexual orientation, internalization, externalization, or age. Conclusions. Among established cigarette smokers, daily ENDS use, compared with some-day or no use, reduced the probability of current smoking. These findings support the potential role of ENDS as a harm reduction tool to facilitate smoking cessation among adults. Keywords: ENDS, e-cigarettes, cigarette cessation, Bayesian additive regression tree, causal inference, adult, Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health Study

after.authors: Ishrat, S.; Nam Le, H.; Yaghooti, B.; Sapkota, R.; Miller, J. P.; Thakuri, D. S.; Bilgel, M.; Resnick, S. M.; Rahmim, A.; Davatzikos, C.; Wong, D. F.; Chand, G.
after.abstract: Introduction Amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) quantifies cerebral {beta}-amyloid in Alzheimer's disease (AD), but tracer- and processing-dependent variability limits comparability. We evaluated Centiloid transformations for multi-atlas segmentation (MUSE)-based [11C]Pittsburgh compound B (PiB) and [18F]florbetapir (AV-45) PET. Methods Standardized uptake value ratio (SUVr) Centiloid transformations without partial-volume correction (NoPVC) and with parallel level set regularization-based PVC (PLS-PVC) were calibrated using the original Klunk Centiloid PiB reference dataset (N = 79) and paired PiB-AV-45 Navitsky dataset (N = 43). Centiloid transformations were evaluated in Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI; AV-45) and secondarily in Knight Alzheimer Disease Research Center (Knight-ADRC; PiB) cohorts. Outcomes included AD-cognitively normal (CN) separation and clinical associations. Scanner effects were examined in ADNI. Results MUSE-derived PiB SUVr measurements corresponded strongly with reference measurements (R2 = 0.963, ICC(A,1) = 0.981), and PiB-AV-45 cross-tracer correspondence was high (R2 = 0.873-0.884). NoPVC separated AD from CN in Knight-ADRC PiB (Hedges' g = 1.907) and ADNI AV-45 (g = 0.892). PLS-PVC yielded similar separation in Knight-ADRC ({Delta}g = -0.027; 95% CI -0.122 to 0.023) and modestly greater separation in ADNI ({Delta}g = 0.053; 95% CI 0.038-0.068). Scanner-associated variance represented 33.5% of total Centiloid variance in ADNI; on scanners other than one older model, AD-CN separation was larger (g = 1.31). Both approaches showed clinical associations. Discussion MUSE Centiloid transformations provide a framework for expressing PiB and AV-45 measurements in Centiloid units across independent cohorts. Scanner and processing differences warrant scanner-specific quality checks and cautious interpretation.

after.author_corresponding_institution: Service de Neurophysiologie Clinique, CHU de Bordeaux, Bordeaux, France; Univ. Bordeaux, CNRS, Institut des Maladies Neurodegeneratives, UMR 5293, Bordeaux, Fra
after.abstract: Adaptive deep brain stimulation could make the treatment of essential tremor more responsive to patients' needs, delivering stimulation when tremor-provoking movements occur rather than continuously, thereby potentially reducing habituation-related loss of efficacy and stimulation-induced adverse effects. Its success, however, depends on neural control signals that remain measurable and meaningful long after surgery, at home rather than in the laboratory, and while stimulation is running. Thalamic local field potentials offer such candidate signals, yet they have largely been characterised intraoperatively or in the early postoperative period, under supervised conditions that reveal little about their behaviour in daily life. We therefore followed nine patients with essential tremor implanted with a sensing-enabled neurostimulator targeting the ventral intermediate nucleus and posterior subthalamic area, combining in-clinic recordings three and six months after surgery with weekly, patient-performed home recordings. We extracted 13 spectral features encompassing canonical and tremor-frequency band power, aperiodic spectral properties and periodic beta activity, and evaluated their agreement between home and clinic recordings, between-session reliability and movement-related modulation across recording settings and stimulation states. Oscillatory features did not differ systematically between home and clinic, whereas the aperiodic background was consistently steeper at home and poorly reproducible. Periodic beta measures emerged as the most robust candidates: with stimulation off, their clinic-home reliability approached that observed between the two clinic visits, and a postural task suppressed beta activity across recording settings, an effect carried by the periodic component rather than by the aperiodic background. Stimulation, however, reduced the reliability of beta measures and markedly attenuated their movement-related modulation, precisely under the conditions in which an adaptive controller would need to operate. Within the limits of this small cohort, thalamic beta activity therefore appears unlikely to serve as a stand-alone control signal for adaptive stimulation in essential tremor, highlighting the potential need for complementary cortical or peripheral inputs.

after.authors: Anim, P. A.; Hammond, E.; Oforiwaa Amanfo, G.; Duku, A.; Kwartemaah Frimpong, A.; Awere Gambrah, D.; Dzomeku, V. .M.
after.abstract: Background: Timely recognition of obstetric danger signs during pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum period is critical for reducing maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality. In Ghana, maternal mortality remains high despite improvements in healthcare, partly due to inadequate awareness of these signs. This study assessed the knowledge and awareness of obstetric danger signs among pregnant women attending antenatal care (ANC) at Kwadaso SDA Hospital. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 200 pregnant women aged 18 years and above, recruited through simple random sampling. Data were collected using structured, interviewer-administered questionnaire adapted from JHPIEGO, covering sociodemographic information, obstetric history, knowledge of danger signs in different pregnancy phases and awareness-related attitudes. Data were analyzed using SPSS version 21, with descriptive statistics, Chi-square tests, and logistic regression used to assess associations. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Results: The most recognized obstetric danger signs were severe vaginal bleeding (97% antepartum, 85% intrapartum, and 92% postpartum) and retained placenta (95% intrapartum). Knowledge was high during the antepartum (86.5%) and intrapartum (78%) periods but dropped to 41% postpartum, resulting in 59% having poor overall knowledge. Women with 1to 3 children [(aOR=3.86, 95% CI: 1.31 to 11.36; p=0.014)] and 4 to 6 children [(aOR=6.12, 95% CI: 1.43 to 26.16; p=0.015)] were more likely to have good knowledge. Those with pregnancy-induced hypertension [(aOR=13.25, 95% CI: 1.10 to159.02; p=0.042)] and women who attended six to nine ANC visits [(aOR=8.98, 95% CI: 1.44 to 56.12; p=0.019)] also demonstrated increased likelihood of good knowledge, while participants with only primary education had lower odds [(aOR=0.06, 95% CI: 0.01 to 0.46; p=0.007)]. Conclusion: Although awareness of some key obstetric danger signs, particularly bleeding, was high, overall knowledge remained inadequate, especially in the postpartum period. Strengthening targeted ANC education, with emphasis on postpartum complications, is essential to improve timely care-seeking and maternal outcomes in this population.

after.title: Preprint: Single-Cell Gene Expression Heritability Informed by Genotype x Cell-Context Interactions
after.authors: Wang, L.; Gusev, A.; Fadil, C.; Wang, L.; Van Dyke, K.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and Harvard Medical School
after.abstract: Most signals from genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of complex traits implicate noncoding variants with putative gene regulatory effects. However, currently identified regulatory variants, particularly expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs), explain only a small fraction of GWAS associations. Moreover, GWAS loci are enriched near evolutionarily constrained genes, whereas constrained genes are depleted of detectable eQTLs, suggesting that weak or context-specific regulatory mechanisms may contribute substantially to disease risk but remain poorly captured by existing approaches. Here, we introduce scHINT (single-cell gene expression Heritability estimation with genotype x context INTeraction), a computationally efficient framework for quantifying cell-level expression heritability and context-dependent genetic regulation from large-scale single-cell data. Applying scHINT to human brain single-nucleus RNA-seq data, we found that genotype-by-cell-state heritability was widespread across brain cell types and, on average, exceeded main genetic heritability, indicating that context-dependent genetic effects explain a substantial fraction of heritable expression variation. GxCell-State heritability was enriched among low-frequency variants and constrained genes, and showed stronger enrichment for functional gene sets and disease heritability than main genetic effects. Using a novel GxCell-State TWAS framework, we identified 68% more disease-risk genes and recapitulated rare-variant burden-test gene TREM2, which was missed by state-agnostic TWAS. In blood, we observed the same direction of enrichment for GxCell-State heritability at constrained genes, but weaker than in brain, suggesting that cell-state-dependent regulation at constrained genes may be more prominent in brain. Finally, extending scHINT to perturbation screens revealed substantial perturbation-by-cell-state effects, highlighting broad context dependence in transcriptional responses.
